items.prompt: Define a review, and state the task’s terms.
items.canonical_answer: A review is an informed judgement of a work, product, event or place, for readers deciding whether to try it. The task’s terms: it is set as a review in every paper of the corpus — one of Section B’s three categories, 600–900 words, twenty-five marks — and the reader the brief names is the audience the criteria and register are chosen for.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: an informed judgement, for readers deciding whether to try it.
The task’s terms — always a review, one of three categories, 600–900 words, twenty-five marks — frame the definition.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Name the sections of a review, and say where the balance lies.
items.canonical_answer: The sections are the introduction, the account of what is reviewed, the evaluation, and the verdict — and the balance leans evaluation, because the reader can see the thing and cannot see the judgement. In a 700-word review the account earns about 150 words and the evaluation takes three times that, with the verdict keeping its room at the end.
marking_guidance: Credit the four features of the shape: introduction, account, evaluation, verdict.
The balance — evaluation weighted, the account brief — is what makes the shape a review’s.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Give the five things fixed when planning a review, in order.
items.canonical_answer: First the context: what it is, where, when, for whom. Second the thing itself: what actually happens, what is sold, what the event contains. Third the criteria: the standards it will be judged by, chosen before the evidence. Fourth the evidence: what happened, quoted or described specifically, for each criterion. Fifth the verdict: the judgement, graded and named for whom it suits. The order is the plan, because criteria chosen after the evidence are criteria the evidence chose.
marking_guidance: Credit the five in order: context, thing, criteria, evidence, verdict.
The order’s reason — criteria before evidence, or the evidence chose them — is the step most answers miss.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between reviewing and recounting, and where does recounting belong?
items.canonical_answer: Reviewing judges; recounting tells. A piece that gives the day’s events in order without weighing them has written an itinerary, not a judgement, and the reader deciding whether to come has been handed a timetable instead of a verdict. Recounting belongs in the review’s account section — briefly, as scaffolding for the evaluation — and the balance is the test: the account is a sixth of the piece, and the weighing is the rest.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: judging against telling in order.
Must say where recounting belongs — the account, briefly — and give the balance test.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A review of a music festival runs: "We arrived at two. The gates opened at three. At four we saw the first band. At six we ate. At eight the headline act came on and they were quite good." What has gone wrong, and what is the cure?
items.canonical_answer: What has gone wrong is the itinerary: the review recounts the day in order — arrival, gates, band, food, headline — and weighs almost nothing, so the reader deciding whether to come has a timetable and one verdict ("quite good") to climb it with. The cure is the plan’s balance turned round: the day gets 150 words of account, and the evaluation takes the rest — the first band judged, the food judged, the headline act judged against the evening’s shape, with the reader given criteria and evidence rather than a schedule.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: the itinerary, with weighing squeezed to one clause.
Must give the cure: the account brief and the evaluation carrying the piece, with judgements in place of timestamps.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A review of a restaurant spends 400 of its 700 words on the drive there, the parking, the table mix-up and the bill’s arithmetic, and closes: "The food was fine." What has gone wrong, and what is the rule for side details?
items.canonical_answer: What has gone wrong is the starved evaluation: the words went to the logistics and the judgements got the leftovers, so the reader deciding whether to eat there has learned a great deal about the parking and almost nothing about the food. The rule for side details is that they belong to the review only when they carry evidence — the bill’s arithmetic belongs if it is being weighed as value, and the drive belongs if the review is about remoteness; otherwise they are diary, not judgement. The cure is the plan: criteria fixed first, so the side details have nowhere to squat.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: side details starving the evaluation of its words.
Must give the rule: a side detail belongs only when it carries evidence for a criterion.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What are criteria in a review, and who chooses them?
items.canonical_answer: Criteria are the standards a review judges by, and they are chosen by the reviewer, stated in the review, and shared with the reader before the verdict is asked of them. A course might be judged by its teaching, its value and its usefulness; a venue by its sound, its sightlines and its service — and the choosing is the reviewer’s first judgement, because what gets measured is what gets weighed.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the reviewer’s chosen, stated standards of judgement.
The choosing is itself a judgement — what gets measured gets weighed — and is worth credit.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is evidentiary logic, and what does it let the reader do?
items.canonical_answer: Evidentiary logic is the review’s spine: every judgement is followed by the evidence that supports it, so the reader can check the reasoning rather than borrow the verdict. "The teaching was worth the fee — when my sauce split, the instructor made me remake it, talking me through the whisk" gives the claim and the proof, and the reader can weigh both; a verdict without its evidence asks to be believed, and a reader deciding whether to spend money prefers to check.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: judgement followed by its supporting evidence.
What it lets the reader do — check the reasoning — is the definition’s purpose.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Here is a bare judgement: "The museum’s planetarium show was excellent." Support it with two specific pieces of evidence.
items.canonical_answer: A model answer: "The planetarium show was excellent on two counts. The projection held its focus to the edges of the dome — the southern sky, usually a smear of light in lesser domes, came out star by star — and the presenter, a working astronomer doing a shift for love, took my son’s question about Venus and answered it for ninety seconds, to the whole room, as though it were the evening’s best question, which by the end it was." (Any two pieces of specific evidence — things that happened, seen, heard, checked — turn the bare judgement into a review’s sentence.)
marking_guidance: Credit the evidence: two specific things the answer names, because the words are the proof.
The strongest answers make the evidence checkable — a moment, a detail, a quote — so the judgement can be weighed rather than borrowed.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A review’s verdict reads: "Overall, an unforgettable night — the best thing I have seen this year." The review’s evidence paragraph described one good song and a long queue. Is the verdict justified? Judge, and say what the verdict needed.
items.canonical_answer: The verdict is not justified by the evidence given. The claim — "the best thing this year" — sits on a paragraph that contains one good song and a queue, and the gap between the claim and its workings is where the reader’s trust falls through: a verdict this size needs the evening’s shape (what else was on), the band’s form against expectation, and some sense of what "best" is being measured against. The evidence does not have to be endless, but it has to be proportionate — and one song plus a queue is a two-star paragraph carrying a five-star verdict. However, the single song may genuinely have been unforgettable; the defect is not dishonesty but proportion, and the fix is either more evidence or a smaller claim.
marking_guidance: Credit the judgement: not justified, with the reason drawn from the proportion between claim and evidence.
Credit the case for its strength, however: the one song may have been genuinely unforgettable, so the defect is proportion, not honesty.
The strongest answers name the fix — more evidence or a smaller claim — which is what a review’s verdict is always choosing between.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A review of a hotel reads: "Facilities include a pool, a gym, a bar, a restaurant and free wifi." What is the sentence doing, and what does it owe?
items.canonical_answer: The sentence is listing: a contents page where a judgement was owed, and it costs the review its purpose, because the reader deciding whether to stay has been told the hotel exists and nothing about whether it is any good. It owes each item its evaluation — the pool judged (deep? warm? crowded at six?), the gym judged (machines that work? opening hours that suit a jet-lag?), the wifi judged (fast enough for the call home?) — or it owes them their deletion, because in a review every named item costs words it must pay back in judgement.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: the list without judgements, a contents page in place of a review.
Must say what it owes: each item evaluated, or removed — words paid back in judgement.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is evaluative lexis, and why must it be graded?
items.canonical_answer: Evaluative lexis is the vocabulary of judgement — words that say how good, how bad, and in what way, rather than the general praise that could attach to anything. It must be graded because the grade names the level: adequate, strong, outstanding on one ladder; disappointing, weak, dire on the other — and a review that only says "good" and "bad" has a scale with two rungs, which tells the reader almost nothing about where the thing stands.
marking_guidance: Credit the meaning: the vocabulary of judgement, saying how good and in what way.
The grading — the ladder from adequate to outstanding — is what makes the lexis informative.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Give a graded scale of evaluative vocabulary, from the adequate to the outstanding and from the disappointing to the dire.
items.canonical_answer: Up the ladder: adequate (does what it says, no more), solid, strong, excellent, outstanding (sets the standard others are measured by). Down the ladder: underwhelming, disappointing (promised more than it delivered), weak, poor, dire (not worth the money or the journey at all). Each rung is a different judgement, and the review’s words place the thing on the ladder precisely enough for the reader to know where it stands.
marking_guidance: Credit the features of both ladders, with several rungs each, named in order.
The rungs must be genuinely graded — a list of synonyms has a scale with one rung.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Here is a vague evaluation: "The show was really good and the venue was nice." Rewrite it with precise evaluative lexis.
items.canonical_answer: A rewrite: "The show was outstanding in its second half — the two leads found a pace the first act never threatened — and the venue was underwhelming for the price: sightlines that made the stage a rumour from row K, and a bar queue that outlasted the interval." (Any rewrite that replaces "really good" and "nice" with graded, particular judgements — each naming its level and its way of being good or bad — meets the task.)
marking_guidance: Credit the rewrite: graded words replacing the vague ones, because the words are the proof.
The strongest answers split the judgement into its parts — the second act outstanding, the venue underwhelming — so the lexis does the weighing.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: What is the difference between a balanced verdict and a list of likes and dislikes, and what does the reader get from each?
items.canonical_answer: A balanced verdict is a weighed judgement: it names the best and the worst and says which the reader should weight — for whom the thing is worth it, and for whom it is not. A list of likes and dislikes is a tally, and a tally is not a judgement: the reader must do the weighing themselves, which is the job they came to the review to have done. The verdict’s last sentences are its terms — who should come, who should not, why — and that is what the reader of a verdict gets that the reader of a tally does not.
marking_guidance: Must state the contrast: a weighed judgement with terms against a tally left to the reader.
Must say what the reader gets: the weighing done, and the action named — who comes, who does not.
items.provenance: Authored for the YYeni 9093 AS build from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A review reads: "I personally loved the spicy dishes and I personally didn’t like the music. That’s just my opinion!" What has gone wrong, and what would make it a review?
items.canonical_answer: What has gone wrong is taste without an argument: the sentences report the reviewer’s reactions and refuse to justify them, so the reader learns what one person enjoyed and nothing about whether they would enjoy it — which is the question the review exists to answer. What would make it a review is criteria and evidence: the spicy dishes judged (against what a kitchen of this price should do, with a dish named and described), the music judged (too loud for the room? wrong genre for the crowd? with the moment that showed it) — and the "just my opinion" shrug deleted, because a review’s opinion is its product and it owes the reader its reasons.
marking_guidance: Must name the mistake: taste reported without criteria, evidence or argument.
Must give the fix: criteria and evidence in the sentences, and the shrug deleted — the opinion is the product.

items.prompt: Write a review of a one-day first-aid course you attended, for a website that lists local courses. Judge it against criteria the review declares, support every judgement with specific evidence, and end with a verdict on terms the reader can act on. Use 600–900 words. [25]
items.canonical_answer:
A Saturday in a school hall: I spent a day learning to save a life, and I want to tell you — precisely — what my money bought.
The course is a one-day emergency first-aid certificate, run eight times a year in the hall of the Omuramba primary school, from eight to four, for N$850 including lunch and a manual. I came as a parent with no medical background and a fair amount of scepticism about how much a Saturday can teach. I left with a certificate, a set of reflexes I did not have in the morning, and two things to say about the day’s quality.
My criteria, declared early so you can check me: was it taught by someone who could teach, does what it teaches survive the adrenaline of a real emergency, and is it worth what it costs against the alternatives.
First, the teaching. Our instructor, a retired paramedic named Katrina with thirty years of the wrong kind of mornings behind her, did the thing that separates a teacher from a presenter: she made us fail. The manikins arrived in the first five minutes and we were compressing within the hour — badly, all of us, mine especially — and instead of correcting the room’s errors gently, she let each of us feel the elbow-lock give way, the rhythm break, the depth go shallow, and then rebuilt it with the counting trick that I now catch myself doing on steering wheels at red lights. That is teaching: the failure was the syllabus. When my partner’s scenario went wrong in the afternoon — she froze at the bleeds section — Katrina talked her through it the way I imagine she talked through real mornings, and the room watched a paramedic’s calm being learned in front of us.
Second, the survival question, which for a first-aid course is the real one. I cannot prove the reflexes will hold on a pavement. What I can tell you: the day’s last hour is all scenarios, with Katrina and a volunteer playing casualties of escalating difficulty, and the course’s design is honest about adrenaline — it teaches you to say out loud what you are doing, because the saying is the anchor, and it drills the recovery position until the room can do it while talking, which is the condition it will actually be needed in. One criticism: the choking scenario came once, late, and I would have traded ten minutes of the bleeds section for a second run at it.
Third, the value. N$850 for a day, a manual, a lunch and a certificate is at the high end of the market here — the online alternative is a quarter of the price and, I now believe, a quarter of the reflexes. The certificate is accepted by the schools’ volunteer programme, which is why half the hall was parents. I would pay it again.
The verdict, then, on terms: for parents, teachers and anyone who organises other people’s children — outstanding value for money; book it, and book early, because the hall is small. For the general reader with no one to be responsible for — adequate, worth it if the schedule suits. And for anyone who already holds a certificate more than three years old: the drills have changed, and this is the refresher I would send you to.
By four o’clock I could do with my hands what I could not do at eight, and I have since — at a sports day, in September, in the rain — done it once for real, and felt the counting arrive unbidden. The course earns its fee on that sentence alone, and earns this review’s last word: send your Saturday here, and ask Katrina for the morning seat.

Expression and range: credit assured expression with a broad repertoire of structures and vocabulary, some complex or unusual — the model answer is the standard.
Accuracy: credit writing with very few errors and sentence boundaries kept throughout.
Organisation and development: the review’s sections present — introduction, account, evaluation, verdict — with the evaluation weighted, each judgement developed with its evidence.
Task achievement: criteria stated and used, every judgement supported by specific evidence, the verdict balanced and graded with terms the reader can act on, inside 600–900 words.
A Level 3 answer would be clear and correct, the review achieved with some criteria and evidence — but with more recounting, fewer grades, and a verdict closer to a tally.

items.prompt: Write a review of a live theatre performance, for an arts magazine’s readers. Judge it against criteria the review declares, support every judgement with specific evidence, and end with a verdict on terms the reader can act on. Use 600–900 words. [25]
items.canonical_answer:
The State Theatre’s production of The Long Rains played two nights only, and this review is written for the people who missed it — because they are the audience it deserves next.
The play is a two-act family drama set on a farm in a bad season, staged with a cast of four in the round, in the theatre’s smaller auditorium, for two hours ten with an interval. I want to be even-handed about the evening, because it was two evenings’ worth of a production: one that deserves the praise it will get and one that the second act did to itself.
The first act was outstanding. The set — designed, the programme says, by a second-year student — is a single invention: the farmhouse kitchen on a revolve that the family turns by hand as the seasons argue, so the room itself becomes the argument, and the cast’s hands on the revolve are the best piece of physical theatre I have seen here in years. The mother, played by Naledi Shipanga, holds the act together the way weather holds a season together: her monologue about the borehole — delivered to the dark above the audience, not to us, which was the choice — made the row in front of me stop eating their sweets, which is the theatre’s only honest standing ovation.
And then the interval, and then the second act, and I want to describe the fall accurately rather than rudely. The pacing goes: what the first act builds across ninety minutes, the second act resolves in twenty-five, and the last five minutes of the play — a reunion the programme calls earned and I call scheduled — undid some of my faith in the writing rather than the performances, because Shipanga and the son (Tomas Uirab, excellent throughout) played the scene as though they too had expected more road. It is not a bad second act. It is an underwritten one, and the cast visibly knew it.
Criteria, so you can check me: the writing (outstanding act one, underwritten act two), the performances (outstanding, both leads, and the supporting pair gave the farm two of its three best moments), the staging (outstanding — the revolve is the production’s signature and its argument), and the value (two hours of this cast at this price is strong; two hours of this script is adequate).
The verdict, weighed and on terms: go to this company’s next production — it is the most exciting thing in the city’s theatre, and the student-designed set alone is worth the ticket. If this play returns with a rewritten second act, book immediately. If it returns as it is, go for the first act, stay for the performances, and forgive the last five minutes the way you forgive a friend who finishes your sentence badly.
I have one more thing to say about the evening, and it belongs to the venue as much as the play, because a review for the people who missed it should tell them what the room itself does. The smaller auditorium seats a hundred and forty in the round, and the roundness is not a gimmick here: the farm kitchen turns and every quarter of the audience holds a corner of the family’s life for a while, so the play happens to you from four directions over two hours, and the moments that land across the seats — a son’s line delivered to the far side of the room, a silence held for the row behind you — are the production’s private gift to its own space. This play should tour nowhere until it has played this room a third time.
The two nights it played, the theatre was three-quarters full, and the third quarter is the production’s real loss. Someone revive the rains.

items.prompt: Write a review of the new sports centre, for a local news website’s readers. Judge it against criteria the review declares, support every judgement with specific evidence, and end with a verdict on terms the reader can act on. Use 600–900 words. [25]
items.canonical_answer:
The new sports centre on the eastern edge of town has been open four months, and this review is written for the people deciding whether to buy the year’s membership — because I have, and because I nearly did not renew.
The centre is a municipal facility with a twenty-five-metre pool, a gym floor of forty machines, two courts, a cafe and a creche, run on a tiered membership of N$250 a month for off-peak or N$380 for any-time. I have used it four mornings a week since it opened, which is the kind of sample a review can stand on, and my criteria are the three a member actually lives by: is the equipment there and working, is the pool swimmable at the hours it promises, and is the staff-to-member ratio what the price claims.
On the equipment: strong, with one reservation that will matter to you at six in the morning. The gym floor is new — the machines are the newest in the region, the treadmills have screens that work, and the free-weights area is genuinely well designed, with a lifting platform the private gyms in town would envy. The reservation is maintenance tempo: of the forty machines, I have not yet seen more than two out of order at once, but the two are, more often than not, the two you wanted — in four months, the rowing machines have been the recurring casualty, and the repair time has run from two days (June) to eleven (August, with a sign that said ‘soon’ for a week, which is not a repair schedule).
On the pool, which is the membership’s heart: outstanding for the price, with a caveat about the clock. The water is the best municipal swimming I have had in this country — properly treated, properly warm (the 27 degrees the board promised, and I have checked it against my own thermometer, which is the kind of person four months of membership makes you), and the morning lanes are respected: the six-to-eight swim is adults, quiet, and the lane etiquette is policed by the lifeguards with a politeness that works. The caveat: the published timetable has the pool to members until seven, and twice in four months the school programme has arrived at six forty-five with a coach who treated the timetable as a suggestion. Both times the front desk handled it, and both times I lost the water I had planned on.
On the staff: adequate to strong, improving. The lifeguards are the centre’s best asset — trained, awake, and one of them (Andreas, mornings) has learned every regular’s name and stroke, which sounds small and is not. The gym floor is supervised in the way that counts: seen but not hovering.
The verdict, on terms. For the swimmer: outstanding value — the pool alone is worth the fee, and the mornings are worth waking for. For the gym member: strong value with a patience requirement — book around the rowing machines and accept the occasional ‘soon’. For the family: strong, with the creche a genuine bonus at this price. And for the municipal board, who will read this if the pattern of the last four months holds: the maintenance tempo is the gap between a centre people recommend and a centre people tolerate, and the membership is watching the sign. One line for the cafe, which the review owes because members plan their mornings around it: the coffee is better than a municipal cafe has any right to be, the bean soup on Tuesdays is worth timing a swim to, and the staff keep the towel-rack area clean past the point of obligation. A small thing, done well, four months in — it is the centre in miniature, and the reason this review wants the sign fixed.

items.prompt: Write a review of a television series you have watched, for your blog’s readers. Judge it against criteria the review declares, support every judgement with specific evidence, and end with a verdict on terms the reader can act on. Use 600–900 words. [25]
items.canonical_answer:
The series everyone at work is talking about has nine episodes, a desert setting and a plot about a border town and its missing water, and I watched all nine in six nights, which is itself part of the review.
This is a review of The Dry Season for the blog’s readers — people who decide what to watch next on a recommendation, and who have been burned before — so I will be exact about what worked, what did not, and which viewers this is for. My criteria: does the plot hold its own logic across nine episodes, do the characters earn their changes, and is the thing worth the six nights it asks of a life.
The plot holds. This is the series’ quiet achievement, and I want to defend it against the reviews calling it slow: the mystery — who signed the water away, and who is making the town pay for it — is structured like the town’s own boreholes, with the truth getting deeper the further down you go, and every episode ends on a discovery that reorganises the one before it. Two episodes in the middle (four and five) sag — the flashbacks to the grandfather’s arrival tell us what episode two implied better — but the ninth pays the whole account, and it pays it with a reveal I did not see and did not feel cheated by, which is the rarest thing the genre does.
The characters earn their changes, mostly. The sheriff, played with magnificent economy by an actress I now want in everything, changes the most and pays the most for it, and the show has the discipline to let her be wrong about the water for two full episodes after the audience has worked it out — the refusal to make her clever for our comfort is what makes her real. The weak joint is the brother: his turn in episode seven is earned by the plot’s logic and not by anything the writing gave him, and the performance does its best with a decision that arrived from the outline rather than the character.
The production: outstanding for its budget, and I say that as someone who knows what a desert costs to shoot in. The wind is a character, the light is a plot device, and the scene in episode eight — the town meeting, one shot, four minutes, no music — is the best television the year has given me, and the reason I am writing this at one in the morning.
The verdict, on terms, and graded. For viewers who like their plots to hold water: outstanding — watch it, and watch it attentively, because the show trusts you and does not re-explain. For viewers who need a sympathetic centre: strong — the sheriff is worth the six nights, but bring patience for the middle. For viewers who watch for pace: adequate — four and five are real, and no one should pretend otherwise. And the six nights: worth it, and worth saying why against the alternatives, because a reader deciding what to watch next is choosing. Against the other desert drama everyone recommended in the spring: this one trusts you more and explains itself less, which is a compliment if you like trust and a warning if you like recaps. Against the comedy in the same list slot: different jobs, different nights. And for the reader who watches alone and wants company: the show’s town meeting scene in episode eight has already done the rounds of my group chat, which is the modern form of a recommendation — the scene people send each other — and it has earned its circulation, because four unbroken minutes of a town arguing about water, with the camera refusing to help, is what the whole medium is for.
The Dry Season is the best thing on the list this month, and episode eight is the reason the list exists.
